newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Assembly approves Robinson as rights chief.
newsitem.headline: UN Assembly approves Robinson as rights chief.

text.p: The 185-member General Assembly on Tuesday approved Ireland's President Mary Robinson as the world's top human rights advocate but left open her starting date.

The endorsement, without a vote, was in response to a note from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan saying he "proposes to appoint Mrs. Mary Robinson (Ireland) as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, for a term of office for four years." Assembly President Razali Ismail said Annan would inform the body of when she would begin the four-year term.

Latin American states and some other developing countries would have preferred the appointment of Sonia Picado, Costa Rica's ambassador to Washington, to succeed Jose Ayala Lasso, the first high commissioner for human rights, who resigned in March to become Ecuador's foreign minister.
Picado indicated to reporters last month, after hearing from Annan that she would not get the top post, that she had been offered the deputy job but probably would not accept it.
Reflecting unhappiness with Robinson's appointment, Costa Rican U.N. Ambassador Fernando Berrocal Soto told the assembly he "would not be participating in the decision" it was about to take.

While recognising the "high merits of the distinguished president of Ireland," he objected to the fact that the Latin American and Caribbean regional group would be deprived of filling the remainder of Ayala Lasso's four-year term, as well as a likely second term. Alluding to Picado, he also regretted that "opportunity was denied to a candidate who also has very high merits, recognised by all."

After Robinson's appointment was endorsed by consensus, Irish Ambassador John Campbell thanked the assembly on her behalf and on behalf of the government and people of Ireland. "Mrs. Robinson will work to serve the high trust that you have placed in her," he added.

In an apparent effort to raise the profile of the human rights activities in the world organisation, Annan last Thursday announced he had chosen Robinson, calling her an "extraordinary leader" who would bring "dynamism to the job."
He wasted little time in getting the assembly to approve his choice, despite reports Third World countries might object to a European.

Annan said last week he had asked Robinson to step down from the Irish presidency by September so she could begin the job at the beginning of the 52nd General Assembly session. But there was no word whether she would do so. Her starting date will be discussed when she meets Annan in New York next month.
One Irish envoy said Robinson would prefer to wait until Dec. 2 when her seven-year term expires but "she is sensitive to the requirements of the secretary-general."

Robinson, 53, a lawyer and human rights legal expert, was the first woman elected president of Ireland. She has used the largely ceremonial post to spotlight injustices in the world and advocate liberalising Ireland's strict divorce and abortion laws, and has travelled to trouble spots such as Somalia at the height of its famine and Rwanda after the 1994 genocide.
Robinson was a member of Ireland's Labour Party but resigned in 1985 over its policy on the Anglo-Irish agreement. The party, however, sponsored her nomination for president.

Ayala Lasso, a low key diplomat, was appointed in 1994 for a four-year term with the support of Third World nations. The post of high commissioner entails running the U.N. human rights centre, which employs 150 people in Geneva and 250 observers in 12 field offices set up by Ayala Lasso.
Robinson will be expected to denounce repressive regimes while trying to get a foothold in countries where U.N. monitoring is needed.
